Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

[{"id": "arka-v3-dev-polish-0020", "row_sha256": "216a5487fc026ecdebe31f6847eb3a3cfa52ecdd2e76381cd65363d092c11ec7", "mode": "/polish", "language": "en", "context": {}, "identity": false, "mode_instructions": "Rewrite awkward phrasing into readable prose for the supplied profile, or plain prose when none is supplied. Preserve intent and certainty. Do not add a greeting, subject, signature, conclusion, or fact that the input did not supply.", "input": "
last october i took the ridgeflow squeeze filter on a three-night trip in the north fork area, and i used it for all the water i drank and cooked with. i bought it myself a few weeks before the trip, so this is not a review from somebody who got sent a sample. the filter is a short, firm plastic tube with a cap on each end, a soft squeeze pouch, and a small backflush syringe in the package. the listed weight is 2.1 ounces, and on my kitchen scale the filter and caps came to just under that, without the pouch. i put the pouch and syringe in a separate pocket on the scale, because i wanted to see what i was actually carrying, not because i think the number on the package is wrong.

The first evening, i filled the pouch at a clear creek and had no trouble getting water through the filter. i did have to push harder than i expected, especially when the pouch was full. after a few squeezes, i got into a rhythm: hold the filter over the bottle, keep the pouch close to the opening, and press steadily instead of trying to empty it all at once. my one-liter bottle took about a minute and a half to fill, though that was my timing and not a test with a stopwatch. the water had no noticeable grit or odd taste to me. i drank it plain and used it later for oatmeal and tea.

On the second day, the creek beside camp had a muddy edge where people had stepped into it. i collected water a little upstream, but the pouch still picked up a few bits of leaf and fine sediment. i let the pouch sit for a minute before filtering, which made the larger pieces easier to avoid. the filter did not clog completely, but the squeeze got slower after several refills. i was not sure how much of that was sediment and how much was me squeezing unevenly. at lunch my friend Mara asked, “Is it supposed to take this much effort?” i said i thought it was normal when the water was cloudy, but i couldn't tell her that with certainty.

1. what worked and what didn't
The caps stayed on in my pack, and i didn't find water leaking from the pouch or filter. The pouch opening was wide enough to fill at the creek without using a cup, although holding it open with cold fingers was fiddly. The filter's clean end fit the narrow mouth of my bottle. It also fit the soft flask i brought, but only if i held the flask steady while squeezing. When i set it down on a flat rock, the flask bent and the connection came loose once. That was my mistake as much as a design problem, but it meant i started holding both pieces together every time.

I liked that i could drink directly from the filter, too. On a steep section, i took a drink from the creek through the filter rather than stopping to fill a bottle. The mouthpiece cover is small and easy to misplace, so i kept it attached to the filter with a short cord i already had. The cord is not included. I didn't measure the flow rate or check the filter with laboratory equipment, and i can't say anything about contaminants that aren't visible or noticeable. I followed the package directions about collecting water and cleaning the filter, but this trip doesn't tell me how long it will last.

Cleaning took a little attention at the end of each day. i drew clean water into the syringe and pushed it back through the filter in the direction the instructions show. The syringe worked, but its plunger felt stiff at first, and i had to press it with both thumbs. after i did it a couple times, the movement got easier. i also tapped the filter gently against my palm before putting the caps back on. The package says not to use soap on the filter, so i didn't. The pouch was harder to dry than the filter itself; when i packed up in the morning, a few drops were still inside the seam.

On the last morning, i used the filter at a small pool below a trail crossing. I couldn't see the bottom, and i tried to scoop from the side where the water was moving rather than from the still center. It took more squeezes than at the clear creek on the first night. I had enough patience to finish filling my bottle, but i was glad i wasn't trying to filter a large pot of water quickly. For cooking, i filtered one pouch at a time into a metal cup and poured it into the pot. It worked, though it made the preparation slower than simply using water from a tap at home.

My main complaint is the effort needed to squeeze, especially with cold hands or water that carries sediment. The pouch is useful and lightweight, but it doesn't feel especially robust when full, and i treated it carefully around rocks. I didn't puncture it or notice a seam separating during this trip. The caps and filter body felt more solid than the pouch. I would bring the filter on another short trip because the whole setup packed small and handled my drinking and cooking water, but i would still give myself extra time at cloudy sources and take care not to lose the mouthpiece cover. It's a practical option for the way i camp, with a few small hassles i now know to expect.", "output": "Last October, I took the Ridgeflow squeeze filter on a three-night trip in the North Fork area and used it for all the water I drank and cooked with. The caps and filter body felt more solid than the pouch. I’d bring the filter on another short trip because the setup packed small and handled my drinking and cooking water. I’d still allow extra time at cloudy sources and take care not to lose the mouthpiece cover. It’s a practical option for the way I camp, with a few small hassles I now know to expect."}]
